findings.current_part: SW1 = Nidec Copal CSS series compact slide switch. Verified from the Nidec CSS catalogue: contact rating non-switching DC50 V / 100 mA, switching DC12 V / 100 mA, minimum DC20 mV / 1 uA; contact resistance 70 mohm maximum; insulation resistance 100 Mohm min at DC500 V; slider contact, fixed contact and terminal pin are copper alloy, gold-plated; cover SUS304 stainless; 2 mm stroke. Netlist (pinout dump of the fork board): SW1.1 = VBATT, SW1.2 = SW, SW1.3 = SW, SW1.4 = unconnected. The SW net goes ONLY to Q3 emitter, R3 (5.1k), R11 (1k), R12 (100k), R58 (5.1k) and TP20 — a soft-start / enable network. Meanwhile VBATT feeds PTC1 directly, and PTC1.2 = VCC feeds U5 VIN/VIN1/VIN2, L1, L2 and C37. So the converter input is permanently connected to the pack and the switch only gates the LTC3527's SHDN pins via /EN.
findings.proposal: No change. Reporting the answer to the question, because it removes an obvious-looking lever from consideration.
findings.benefit: Zero, and I want to be explicit rather than inflate it. SW current computed from the netlist at V_pack = 3.0 V: R3 5.1k + R4 33k = 38.1k -> 79 uA; R58 5.1k + R63 100k = 105.1k -> 28.5 uA; R11 1k + R24 100k = 101k -> 30 uA; R12 100k -> up to 30 uA when Q1 conducts. Total ~140-170 uA. Dissipation in SW1 at its 70 mohm maximum contact resistance = (170e-6)^2 x 0.070 = 2.0e-9 W = 0.000002 mW. Voltage drop across the contacts = 170 uA x 70 mohm = 12 uV. This is nine orders of magnitude below anything that matters. It is also good design: the stock GBA switches the full battery current through its power switch, whereas AGBM-01 uses the switch only as a logic-level enable, which is why the switch's 100 mA contact rating is not a problem despite the board drawing up to 780 mA. Corollary worth stating: do NOT 'fix' this by routing VBATT through SW1 — that would exceed the switch's 100 mA switching rating by roughly 8x at the overclocked peak. The switch also stays comfortably above its DC20 mV / 1 uA minimum applicable load, and the contacts are gold-plated, so dry-circuit film formation is not a concern.
findings.risk: None. The only downstream consequence of the topology is that the pack is never fully disconnected: with SW1 off, the always-on drain is R9 (100k, VBATT to VFILT) feeding U3's supervisor plus U5's shutdown quiescent current (LTC3827 datasheet gives 0.1 uA typ / 2 uA max in shutdown, not including switch leakage). That is a few microamps at 3 V, i.e. single-digit microwatts — irrelevant against a ~2000 mAh AA pair.
findings.verify_reason:
Every switch specification is CONFIRMED verbatim. I fetched and text-extracted the Nidec Copal CSS catalogue: Contact rating 'Non-switching: DC50 V, 100 mA / Switching: DC12 V, 100 mA / Minimum: DC20 mV, 1 uA'; Contact resistance '70 mOhm maximum'; Insulation resistance '100 MOhm minimum (DC500 V)'; Internal structure table gives Slider contact, Fixed contact and Terminal pin as 'Copper alloy, Gold-plated' and Cover as 'Stainless steel (SUS 304)'; Stroke 2 mm. All exact.

The topology claim is the important one and it is correct. I re-dumped the nets: SW1.1 = VBATT, SW1.2 = SW, SW1.3 = SW, SW1.4 unconnected. The SW net has exactly 8 pads: Q3.2 (emitter), R3.1, R11.1, R12.1, R58.1, SW1.2, SW1.3, TP20. Meanwhile VBATT feeds PTC1.1 directly and PTC1.2 = VCC feeds U5 VIN/VIN1/VIN2, L1, L2 and C37. The converter input is permanently connected to the pack and SW1 gates only the enable network. So no load current passes through the switch, and the switch's 100 mA rating is not a problem despite a 780 mA peak board draw.

The corollary is the most valuable part of the finding and I endorse it: routing VBATT through SW1 would exceed its 100 mA switching rating by ~8x at the overclocked peak. That is a genuine trap this finding closes off.

One thing worth adding for the reviewer: I found that the PCB's R3 value (1k) disagrees with the schematic's (5.1k) and R4's (10k vs 33k) — see f1-ptc1-value-conflict. Both are on this exact network, so anyone recomputing these currents from the layout will get different numbers again. It does not change the answer (nanowatts either way) but it is worth knowing.

CONFIRMED — no change recommended, and the finding is right to state the saving as zero rather than dress it up.
findings.correction:
Two errors of detail, neither of which touches the conclusion.

(1) The part name is wrong in the risk paragraph: 'LTC3827 datasheet gives 0.1 uA typ / 2 uA max in shutdown'. The converter is the LTC3527 (LTC3827 is an unrelated dual step-down controller). The numbers happen to be right for the LTC3527 — I extracted the datasheet (35271fc): 'Quiescent Current: Shutdown, VSHDN1 = VSHDN2 = 0V, Not Including Switch Leakage, VOUT1 = VOUT2 = 0V: 0.1 typ, 2 max, uA'. Note the exclusion the finding repeats but does not follow through: the adjacent line 'NMOS Switch Leakage Current, VSW1,2 = 5V, SHDN1,2 = 0V: 0.1 typ, 10 max uA' is additional, so the true off-state drain can be up to ~12 uA rather than ~2 uA. Still microwatts. Conclusion unaffected.

(2) The SW-net current estimate is low by roughly 2x because it omits Q3's base path. Q3 (2N3906 PNP) has its emitter on SW and its base tied through R15 (10k) to Q1's collector; when Q1 conducts, that path draws roughly (3.0 - 0.7)/10k = 230 uA out of SW — larger than any of the four resistor legs the finding counted. Realistic SW current is ~0.15-0.4 mA, not 0.14-0.17 mA. Redoing the dissipation at the pessimistic end: (400e-6)^2 x 0.070 = 1.1e-8 W = 0.00001 mW, and the contact drop is 28 uV. Eight to nine orders of magnitude below relevance, exactly as the finding concludes.

Also: 'the stock GBA switches the full battery current through its power switch' is uncited and I did not verify it. It is contextual colour, not a spec claim.

findings.title: SW1's value "CSS-1310B" is not a complete Nidec Copal ordering code — the SMD gull-wing part is CSS-1310TB
findings.current_part: Schematic and PCB Value = "CSS-1310B". The Nidec CSS catalogue's part-number designation is CSS - (poles)(contacts)(setting position)(self-return) (packaging) (terminal shape), where packaging is T = taping or M = magazine and terminal shape is B = gull wing or C = through-hole pins. The catalogue's LIST OF PART NUMBERS for the 3-contact side-setting no-self-return variant contains exactly two entries: CSS-1310TB (gull wing, taping, 1900 pcs/reel) and CSS-1310MC (through-hole pins, magazine, 38 pcs/stick). "CSS-1310B" omits the packaging letter and does not appear in the list.
findings.proposal: CSS-1310TB. The board footprint Bucketmouse:AGB-Switch_CSS-1X10B_Uncentered places SMD rectangular pads on B.Cu, i.e. gull-wing terminals, so the B (gull wing) / T (tape) part is the right one. AGBM-11 uses an even looser value, "CSS-1X10B", so this is a house shorthand rather than a typo, but a builder searching a distributor for "CSS-1310B" gets nothing.
findings.benefit: No electrical effect. Purely a BOM-usability fix.
findings.risk: None. Worth a two-second edit next time the schematic is touched.
findings.verify_reason:
Verified from the Nidec Copal CSS catalogue that I fetched and text-extracted:

Part-number designation scheme, quoted verbatim from the catalogue's own worked example 'C S S - 1 2 1 1 T B': Series name / No. of poles (1 = 1 pole) / No. of contacts (2 = 2 contacts, 3 = 3 contacts) / Setting position (0 = top, 1 = side) / Self-return function (0 = none, 1 = single, 2 = double) / Form of packaging (T = taping, M = magazine) / Shape of terminal (B = gull wing, C = through hole pins). Exactly as the finding describes.

LIST OF PART NUMBERS: for the 3-contact, side-setting, no-self-return row the only two entries are CSS-1310TB (1,900 pcs/reel) and CSS-1310MC (38 pcs/stick). Confirmed, including the packaging quantities.

Footprint check, done independently in the PCB file: Bucketmouse:AGB-Switch_CSS-1X10B_Uncentered has five pads, all (pad ... smd rect ... (size 1 2.8) (layers "B.Cu" "B.Mask" "B.Paste")). SMD rectangular pads on the bottom copper — a gull-wing surface-mount part, so the B / T (gull wing, taping) variant is the right one and CSS-1310TB is the correct order code. Confirmed.

Distributor availability confirmed for CSS-1310TB (DigiKey part 1124228, Arrow, RS, element14); searches for the exact string 'CSS-1310B' return only CSS-1310TB listings, so the finding's practical point — a builder searching that string is on their own — holds.

Zero electrical effect, correct action, one mischaracterisation of the source. REVISED.
findings.correction:
'"CSS-1310B" ... does not appear in the list' is true of the LIST OF PART NUMBERS but the finding then generalises it into 'this is a house shorthand rather than a typo', which is wrong. CSS-1310B is Nidec's OWN designation. The catalogue's OUTLINE DIMENSIONS section is headed with bullets reading '● CSS-1210B', '● CSS-1211B', '● CSS-1311B', '● CSS-1310B', '● CSS-1210C', '● CSS-1312B' — Nidec uses the packaging-less form to label the mechanical drawings, because packaging does not change the outline. So the schematic value is the manufacturer's own outline designation with the packaging letter omitted, not a MouseBiteLabs invention. AGBM-11's looser 'CSS-1X10B' IS a house shorthand; AGBM-01's is not.

The corrective action is unchanged and correct: put CSS-1310TB in the BOM.

findings.title: Board copper from BT1 to the LTC3527 is about 6 mohm — 2-5% of the series path. Leave it alone.
findings.current_part: 4-layer board, 35 um (1 oz) copper on F.Cu, In1.Cu, In2.Cu and B.Cu per the stackup block in the .kicad_pcb. Sheet resistance = 1.72e-8 ohm.m / 35e-6 m = 0.491 mohm per square. The battery path is almost entirely pour, not track: Net-(BT1-+) has one F.Cu zone (68.45 mm2 filled, bbox 13.9 x 10.5 mm) plus 7.16 mm of 0.4 mm track; VBATT has an F.Cu zone (11.18 mm2 filled) plus 16.5 mm of 0.5 mm track (that track goes to SW1 and D2, not the load); VCC has an F.Cu zone (11.64 mm2), two B.Cu zones (22.6 mm2 total) plus 3.75 mm of 1.4 mm B.Cu track, two In2.Cu zones (79.37 + 44.56 = 123.9 mm2) and 12 x 0.7/0.3 mm vias. Key positions: BT1 pad 1 (30.54,-16.47) and (31.00,-18.95); F1 pads (32.14,-24.20)/(30.26,-24.20); PTC1 pads (31.90,-28.54)/(31.90,-26.66); U5 VIN pins around (26.15,-41.35)/(28.35,-39.65); L1 pad 1 (28.32,-45.00); L2 pad 1 (28.32,-34.80).
findings.proposal: No change. Documenting the number so the reviewer does not spend a board revision widening copper that is already 20-40x smaller than the parts it feeds.
findings.benefit:
Segment by segment: (a) BT1+ pour to F1 pad 1, ~6 mm through a pour averaging 6.5 mm wide = ~1 square = 0.5 mohm, call it <=1 mohm. (b) VBATT pour, F1 pad 2 to PTC1 pad 1, 4.4 mm span with 11.18 mm2 filled = ~2.5 mm average width = 1.75 squares = 0.9 mohm. (c) VCC: I ran a scanline resistance integral over the In2.Cu VCC fill polygons (script strip.py in the scratchpad), summing dy/w(y) x R_sheet across the full 21.3 mm from y = -24.40 to -45.68: 3.59 mohm to the far end at L1, and about 2.6 mohm to U5's VIN pins. The parallel B.Cu VCC pour and the 1.4 mm B.Cu track reduce that further, so 2-3.5 mohm is the honest range. (d) Vias: a 0.3 mm drill with 25 um plating over the 1.18 mm stack gives an annulus of 0.0255 mm2 and a full-height resistance of ~0.8 mohm; there are 12 on VCC and 3 on VBATT, in parallel groups, so well under 1 mohm total. (e) Ground return is a solid In1.Cu plane plus GND pours on all four layers — sub-milliohm.
Total one-way: ~5-7 mohm. Loss = I^2 R: 0.24 mW at 200 mA, 0.51 at 292 mA, 0.91 at 390 mA, 1.82 at 550 mA, 3.38 at 750 mA. Against F1 + PTC1's 120-240 mohm, the copper is 2-6% of the series path and nothing to fix.
findings.risk: None. The only caveat is that the scanline integral treats the In2 pour as a 1-D conductor with all the current going to the farthest pin, which overestimates it; the real figure is lower, so 6 mohm is a safe upper bound.
findings.verify_reason:
Everything checkable checks, and I checked the numbers rather than the prose.

Stackup: the .kicad_pcb stackup block gives F.Cu, In1.Cu, In2.Cu and B.Cu all at (thickness 0.035), with dielectrics 0.1 / 0.84 / 0.1 mm. So 35 um copper on four layers and a 1.18 mm copper-to-copper stack — both as stated. Sheet resistance 1.72e-8 / 35e-6 = 0.4914 mOhm/square, correct.

Zones: I enumerated them. Net-(BT1-+) has one F.Cu zone; VBATT has F.Cu and B.Cu zones; VCC has F.Cu, two B.Cu and two In2.Cu zones. Matches.

Track lengths: I summed them from the segment records. Net-(BT1-+) = 2.67 + 0.11 + 2.86 + 1.51 + 0.01 = 7.16 mm at 0.4 mm width — exactly the figure quoted. VBATT = 2.95 + 1.25 + 1.41 + 0.57 + 0.25 + 2.99 + 7.04 + 0.04 = 16.50 mm at 0.5 mm — exactly the figure quoted, and those segments run from x ~5 to x ~13, i.e. toward SW1 at (22.5, -13.1), confirming the parenthetical that this track feeds SW1 and D2 and not the load. VCC B.Cu 1.4 mm segments total 3.76 mm, matching '3.75 mm of 1.4 mm B.Cu track'.

Pad coordinates: BT1 pad 1 at (30.54, -16.47) and (31.00, -18.95); F1 (32.138, -24.200)/(30.262, -24.200); PTC1 (31.900, -26.663)/(31.900, -28.538); U5 VIN region (26.15, -41.348) and (28.348, -40.65); L1 pad 1 (28.325, -45.000); L2 pad 1 (28.325, -34.800). All match to the quoted precision.

Via arithmetic redone: annulus = pi x (0.175^2 - 0.150^2) = 0.02553 mm^2, and R = 1.72e-8 x 1.18e-3 / 2.553e-8 = 7.95e-4 ohm = 0.795 mOhm. Both figures correct.

The conclusion — copper is a few milliohms against 120-230 mOhm of F1+PTC1, so 2-4% of the series path, and widening it is not worth a board revision — is right and is the useful output. CONFIRMED, with the estimate revised slightly downward.
findings.correction:
Two geometric errors, both of which INFLATE the estimate, so the conclusion is safe:

(1) 'VBATT pour, F1 pad 2 to PTC1 pad 1, 4.4 mm span'. I computed the actual pad centres from the footprint origins and rotations: F1 pad 2 = (30.262, -24.200), PTC1 pad 1 = (31.900, -26.663). Span = sqrt(1.638^2 + 2.463^2) = 2.96 mm, not 4.4 mm. Segment (b) is therefore ~0.6 mOhm, not 0.9.

(2) 'summing dy/w(y) x R_sheet across the full 21.3 mm from y = -24.40 to -45.68'. VCC does not start at y = -24.40 — current enters VCC at PTC1 pad 2, which is at (31.900, -28.538). The run to L1 pad 1 at (28.325, -45.000) is 16.5 mm, not 21.3 mm. Segment (c) is correspondingly ~22% smaller than the 3.59 mOhm quoted.

Corrected total: roughly 4-5 mOhm one way rather than 5-7. Loss at 292 mA falls from 0.51 to ~0.38 mW, at 750 mA from 3.38 to ~2.5 mW. The finding's own framing ('6 mOhm is a safe upper bound') survives intact.

findings.title: The battery contacts are the one series element with no published spec, and the cells' own 0.3-0.6 ohm ESR dwarfs everything on the board
findings.current_part: BT1 = Bucketmouse:AGB-Battery, four through-hole pads (two per polarity, 2 x 3.5 mm oval and 2 x 2 mm custom, 1.2 mm drills, on all copper layers). The schematic Source field points at retrogamerepairshop's GBA replacement battery contact terminals. I could find NO published contact-resistance figure for that part or for OEM GBA terminals — the vendor page and the aftermarket listings describe them only qualitatively ('specs very close to OEM', 'reduce electrical resistance'). Treat any number for these contacts as UNVERIFIED.
findings.proposal: Two actions, both free. (1) Measure rather than guess: with the console running at a known current, measure the DC drop from the AA cell's own terminal to the BT1 pad on the PCB, and divide. That converts the unknown into a number in about a minute and tells you whether it belongs in this domain's budget at all. (2) If the contacts are visibly oxidised or corroded — which is the normal state of a 20-year-old GBA — clean or replace them, because that is a zero-cost change with a potentially larger effect than every component swap in this review combined.
findings.benefit: Cannot be quantified from published data, and I am not going to invent a number. What I CAN anchor is the surrounding context: the Energizer E91 datasheet gives nominal internal resistance of 150-300 mohm per fresh AA alkaline, so the pack contributes 300-600 mohm of series resistance — 2 to 5 times the entire board-side path (120-240 mohm as built, 65-115 mohm after the recommended swaps). At the 750 mA overclocked peak the cells alone drop 225-450 mV and dissipate 169-338 mW internally, versus 90-180 mV and 68-135 mW on the board. That is the honest framing for this whole domain: the board-side loss is real and worth attacking, but the pack's own ESR is the dominant term and cannot be touched. It also means contact resistance would have to be in the tens of milliohms per interface before it rivals the cells; on a clean pair of contacts it will not be, and on a corroded pair it may exceed everything else on this list. Note this also means the input path is where a switch to NiMH cells would change the picture, since NiMH ESR is far lower — but I have not verified a NiMH ESR figure so I will not put a number on it.
findings.risk: None. The risk is analytical: if you do not measure the contacts, you may spend a board revision on 20 mohm of PPTC while a corroded terminal is contributing more.
findings.verify_reason:
This is the finding I most expected to fall over on an unsourced number, and it does not — because it refuses to invent one.

The one hard anchor is verified exactly. I fetched and text-extracted the Energizer E91 product datasheet (Form No. E91NA1018): 'Nominal IR: 150 to 300 milliohms (fresh)', with Nominal Voltage 1.5 volts, designation ANSI-15A / IEC-LR6. So 300-600 mOhm for a series pair is correct and correctly attributed.

Arithmetic redone at 750 mA: cell drop 0.75 x 0.30 = 225 mV to 0.75 x 0.60 = 450 mV; internal dissipation 0.5625 x 0.30 = 169 mW to 338 mW. Both correct. Board side: with the corrected R1max of 0.150 the series path is 0.120-0.230 ohm, giving 90-173 mV and 68-129 mW (the finding said 90-180 mV / 68-135 mW, which used the slightly-too-high 0.240 ohm). The framing — cells are 2-5x the board-side path and cannot be touched — survives that correction unchanged.

BT1 footprint verified in the PCB: four pads, two per polarity, at (30.54, -16.47) / (31.00, -18.95) for pad 1 and (31.07, -12.66) / (31.49, -10.18) for pad 2, all through-hole on all copper layers. Matches.

I independently looked for a contact-resistance figure for the retrogamerepairshop replacement terminals or for OEM AGB terminals and found none either. The finding is right to declare it unverified rather than estimate it, and right that a measurement takes a minute and settles it.

The honesty here is the value: it correctly identifies that the pack's own ESR dominates everything on the board, which is the right context for sizing every other finding in this domain. The NiMH remark is properly flagged as unverified and no number is attached. CONFIRMED.

findings.title: Evaluated and rejected: an ideal-diode / eFuse in place of F1+PTC1 is verifiably WORSE at 1.8 V pack voltage
findings.current_part: F1 + PTC1 in series, 0.120-0.240 ohm as built, 0.065-0.115 ohm after the recommended swaps. The attraction of an eFuse or ideal diode is that it would collapse overcurrent protection, reverse-battery protection and the series drop into one part.
findings.proposal: Rejected, with numbers. The obvious candidate is the TI LM66100 (5.5 V, 1.5 A ideal diode with input polarity protection, SC-70-6/DCK), whose recommended input range starts at 1.5 V, low enough for a 2 x AA pack. But its on-resistance is specified against VIN, and it degrades badly at the bottom of the pack: R_ON at IOUT = -200 mA is 79 mohm typ / 95 mohm max at VIN = 5 V; 91 typ / 110 max at 3.6 V; and 141 mohm typ / 180 mohm max at 25 C at VIN = 1.8 V, rising to 210 mohm over -40 to 85 C. At the operating point that matters most — low battery, high current — a single LM66100 is worse than the two parts it would replace and roughly 3x the upgraded pair. Its quiescent current is excellent (0.15 uA typ, 0.3 uA max) but that is not the constraint here. The other family, integrated eFuses with current limiting (TPS259x class), generally do not operate below ~2.7 V, so they are simply out of range for a pack that reaches 1.8 V. A discrete series FET (P-channel on the high side or N-channel in the ground return) faces the same physics — you need R_ds(on) specified at V_GS = 1.8 V, and I could not verify a SOT-23 part whose datasheet specifies R_ds(on) at that gate drive below the 15-65 mohm of the upgraded PPTC, so I will not name one. It would also add no overcurrent protection and would lift the board ground off the battery negative, which complicates the audio-jack reference.
findings.benefit: Negative. Replacing 0.065-0.115 ohm with 141-210 mohm would COST, not save: at 390 mA the delta of roughly +0.07 to +0.13 ohm is 11-20 mW, and at 750 mA it is 39-73 mW.
findings.risk: The value of this finding is that it closes off a plausible-sounding direction with a verified datasheet number rather than an opinion. If the design ever moved to a lithium cell (AGBM-11 territory, 3.0-4.2 V) the LM66100's 91 mohm at 3.6 V becomes competitive and the conclusion would flip — so this rejection is specific to the 2 x AA voltage range.
findings.verify_reason:
I re-derived every LM66100 number from the TI datasheet (SLVSEZ8A, March 2019, revised June 2019) that I fetched and text-extracted, and all of them are exactly right:

- 'Wide operating voltage range: 1.5 V - 5.5 V' — so the 2xAA range is in spec, as the finding says.
- Reverse voltage standoff on VIN: -6 V absolute maximum. Maximum continuous current 1.5 A.
- RON, IOUT = -200 mA: VIN = 5 V, 79 typ / 95 max at 25 C, 110 max over -40..85 C, 120 over -40..125. VIN = 3.6 V, 91 / 110, 125, 140. VIN = 1.8 V, 141 typ / 180 max at 25 C, 210 mOhm over -40..85 C, 230 over -40..125. Every figure the finding cites is verbatim from the table, including the 210 mOhm over-temperature number.
- IQ,VIN: 0.15 typ / 0.3 max uA at 25 C. Correct.
- Package: 'The LM66100 is available in a standard SC-70 package', DCK, 6-pin. Correct.

The TPS259x claim also checks: the TI datasheet is titled 'TPS2595xx 2.7 V to 18 V, 4-A, 34-mOhm eFuse', confirming the family does not operate down to 1.8 V. So that branch is correctly closed.

The discrete-FET paragraph is the right kind of restraint: it identifies the actual constraint (you need Rds(on) specified at VGS = 1.8 V, and most SOT-23 datasheets do not characterise that low), declines to name a part it could not verify, and correctly notes that a ground-return N-channel would lift board ground off the battery negative — which matters here because P3 (SJ-3524-SMT) references AGND and NT1 ties AGND to GND at a single point.

This is the most rigorous finding in the set: it closes a plausible-sounding direction with verified datasheet numbers, states the saving as negative, and scopes the conclusion to the 2xAA voltage range with a correct note that it would flip for AGBM-11's 3.0-4.2 V lithium. CONFIRMED.
findings.correction: One looseness worth flagging, not enough to revise. 'Replacing 0.065-0.115 ohm with 141-210 mOhm ... at 390 mA the delta of roughly +0.07 to +0.13 ohm is 11-20 mW'. The honest bracket is wider: the delta ranges from +0.026 ohm (0.115 -> 0.141, best case both ends) to +0.145 ohm (0.065 -> 0.210, worst case both ends), i.e. 4.0 to 22.1 mW at 390 mA and 14.6 to 81.6 mW at 750 mA. The finding's quoted band sits inside that and its sign never changes, so the conclusion is unaffected: at every pairing the LM66100 costs power rather than saving it.

findings.title: F1 and PTC1 pads use thermal relief to their pours — worth ~0.5 mohm, but solid connections would also raise the PPTC's effective hold current
findings.current_part: Both F1 pads and both PTC1 pads carry (zone_connect 1) with (thermal_bridge_width 0.5), i.e. KiCad thermal relief with 0.5 mm spokes, against the F.Cu BT1+, VBATT and VCC pours. Pads are 0.975 x 1.4 mm roundrect. Zone thermal gap is the KiCad default.
findings.proposal: Set zone_connect 2 (solid fill) on all four pads. PCB file edit only, no land pattern change, no schematic change.
findings.benefit: Small and I will not inflate it. Four spokes of 0.5 mm across a ~0.5 mm gap is 2 mm of effective width over 0.5 mm = 0.25 square = 0.12 mohm per pad; if only two spokes form, 0.25 mohm. Across four pads that is 0.5-1.0 mohm, worth 0.04-0.09 mW at 292 mA and 0.28-0.56 mW at 750 mA. Rounding error on its own. The reason to do it anyway is thermal, not electrical: a PPTC's hold current is set entirely by how fast it sheds heat, and Littelfuse specify I_hold in 20 C still air with no board heatsinking assumed. Bonding both PTC1 pads solidly to the VBATT and VCC pours (11-12 mm2 of F.Cu each, plus the 124 mm2 In2.Cu VCC plane through the vias) gives the device a real heatsink and pushes its effective hold current up, which is exactly the margin the ClockxControl is eating into. Same argument in reverse for F1: solid pads make the fuse slightly slower to open, which is a mild negative, so if you only change one, change PTC1.
findings.risk: Solid pads on 0805 parts are marginally harder to hand-solder and slightly more prone to tombstoning in reflow because the two ends heat unevenly — though with a large pour on both ends that asymmetry is small here. For F1 specifically, better heatsinking raises its effective rating, i.e. slows the fuse; that is a small protection regression, so restricting the change to PTC1 is the conservative option. I have no measured data on how much the effective hold current actually rises, so treat that part as directional, not quantified.
findings.verify_reason:
What is verified and correct: all four pads do carry thermal relief. F1 pads 1 and 2 and PTC1 pads 1 and 2 each have (zone_connect 1) with (thermal_bridge_width 0.5), pads 0.975 x 1.4 mm roundrect. Confirmed from the PCB file.

I also verified the premise that matters most, which the finding did not state: the spokes actually carry the current, because there is no parallel track. I enumerated every track segment on Net-(BT1-+), VBATT and VCC. The VBATT tracks all run between x = 5 and x = 13 (toward SW1 at x = 22.5) and the VCC tracks are on B.Cu at x ~ 23-28; none of them land on F1's or PTC1's pads at x ~ 30-32. So those pads are zone-connected only and the thermal relief is the sole conduction path on F.Cu. The finding's premise holds.

Sheet resistance basis re-derived: 1.72e-8 / 35e-6 = 0.4914 mOhm/square, consistent with the copper-adequate finding.

The recommendation itself (zone_connect 2 on PTC1's pads, PCB edit only, no land pattern or schematic change) is harmless and correctly graded as a PCB revision. But with the corrected geometry the electrical case is 0.03 mW — genuinely rounding error, as the finding itself says — and the thermal case is unquantified and cuts both ways. I would not open the layout for this alone; fold it into an unrelated respin if one happens. REVISED.
findings.correction:
The stated zone geometry is wrong and the benefit is half what is claimed.

'Zone thermal gap is the KiCad default.' It is not. I read the zone records: the F.Cu Net-(BT1-+) and VBATT zones carry (thermal_gap 0.25) (thermal_bridge_width 0.25), and the F.Cu VCC zone carries (thermal_gap 0.25) (thermal_bridge_width 0.25). KiCad's default thermal_gap is 0.5 mm, so this design explicitly halved it. The pad-level override (thermal_bridge_width 0.5) on all four F1/PTC1 pads wins for spoke width, so the real geometry is 0.5 mm spokes across a 0.25 mm gap, not across 0.5 mm.

Recomputed: 4 spokes x 0.5 mm = 2.0 mm effective width over a 0.25 mm gap = 0.125 square = 0.061 mOhm per pad (0.123 mOhm if only two spokes form). Across four pads that is 0.25-0.5 mOhm, not 0.5-1.0. Worth 0.021-0.043 mW at 292 mA and 0.14-0.28 mW at 750 mA. Headline 0.06 -> 0.03 mW, overclocked 0.1 -> 0.05 mW.

The thermal half of the argument is unsupported by any source. The cited Newark listing carries no heat-sinking or board-mounting data, and I found no Littelfuse figure quantifying how much pad-to-pour bonding raises effective I_hold for this part. The finding admits this ('treat that part as directional, not quantified') which is the right posture, but it means the ONLY quantified justification for the change is 0.03 mW, i.e. nothing. Also, the asymmetry the finding draws is not real: better heatsinking raises a PPTC's trip current for exactly the same reason it raises its hold current, so improving PTC1's thermal path degrades its protection in the same direction it degrades F1's — the finding notes this for F1 but not for PTC1.

findings.title: None of the AGBM-01 vs AGBM-02 29 mW idle gap comes from this domain — the protection parts are identical on both boards
findings.current_part: AGBM-01 rev 1.2 schematic: F1 = F0805B2R00FSTR, PTC1 = 0805L075SLYR, D1 = D2 = 1SS355VMTE-17, SW1 = CSS-1310B. I pulled the same fields from MouseBiteLabs' AGBM-02 schematic and PCB and they are character-for-character identical (AGBM-02's PCB even carries the correct Values where AGBM-01's carries the stale 0467001.NR strings).
findings.proposal: No change. Recording it so this domain is correctly excluded from the hunt for the 29 mW idle delta.
findings.benefit: Zero saving; a scoping result. AGBM-01 idles at 170 mW and AGBM-02 at 141 mW. At the self-consistent idle current (170 mW / 2.4 V = 71 mA) the entire F1 + PTC1 series path dissipates 0.60-1.20 mW, i.e. 0.35-0.71% of the idle figure — and since both boards carry the same parts, the contribution to the DELTA is exactly zero. The 29 mW must come from the converter (LTC3527 with 2 x 4.7 uH inductors vs 2 x TPS63802 with 0.47 uH), not from the input path. Corollary for the reviewer's framing: the brief asks for the I2R loss as a percentage of the 170 mW idle, but the 200/350/550 mA currents in the brief do not correspond to the idle condition. Reported both ways: at 200 mA the loss is 4.8-9.6 mW (2.8-5.6% of 170 mW, 0.69-1.37% of 700 mW); at 350 mA it is 14.7-29.4 mW (8.6-17.3% / 2.1-4.2%); at 550 mA it is 36.3-72.6 mW (21.4-42.7% / 5.2-10.4%). The physically meaningful pair is the self-consistent one: 0.6-1.2 mW at idle (0.35-0.71%) and 10.2-20.5 mW at 700 mW in-use (1.5-2.9%).
findings.risk: None.
findings.verify_reason:
I verified the scoping claim directly rather than taking it on trust. Extracting the Value properties from MouseBiteLabs' AGBM-02 schematic gives F1 = F0805B2R00FSTR, PTC1 = 0805L075SLYR, D1 = 1SS355VMTE-17, D2 = 1SS355VMTE-17, SW1 = CSS-1310B — character-for-character identical to AGBM-01's schematic, including the same shared Description strings. Confirmed.

I went further and checked the AGBM-02 net topology too, which the finding did not: D1 pad 1 on Net-(BT1-+), F1 Net-(BT1-+) -> VBATT, PTC1 VBATT -> VCC, SW1 VBATT -> SW. Identical arrangement. So the input path is genuinely common to both boards and cannot contribute to the 29 mW idle delta. The scoping conclusion is airtight.

Also confirmed: AGBM-02's PCB carries the correct Values (F0805B2R00FSTR / 0805L075SLYR) where AGBM-01's PCB carries the stale 0467001.NR strings, which is the same cross-design evidence used in f1-ptc1-value-conflict.

Arithmetic redone: 170 mW / 2.4 V = 70.8 mA; 0.0708^2 x 0.120 = 0.601 mW and x 0.230 = 1.15 mW; 0.60/170 = 0.35% and 1.15/170 = 0.68%. 700 mW / 2.4 V = 292 mA; 0.0853 x 0.120 = 10.2 mW and x 0.230 = 19.6 mW. All correct modulo the R1max fix.

The most useful thing here is the methodological correction it makes to the brief — that the 200/350/550 mA currents do not correspond to the 170 mW idle condition, so quoting the loss as a percentage of 170 mW at 550 mA (21-43%) is a category error. Reporting both the self-consistent pair and the literal answer is the right call. CONFIRMED.
findings.correction:
Only the R1max correction propagates. With 0805L075SL's true R1max of 0.150 ohm (not 0.160), the series path is 0.120-0.230 ohm and every upper bound drops ~4%:
  idle, 71 mA: 0.60-1.15 mW (0.35-0.68% of 170 mW)
  200 mA: 4.8-9.2 mW
  350 mA: 14.7-28.2 mW
  550 mA: 36.3-69.6 mW
  292 mA (700 mW in use): 10.2-19.6 mW (1.5-2.8%)
The delta contribution remains exactly zero either way, since both boards carry the same parts.

findings.title: CP1/CP2/CP3 are polarized tantalums on a symmetric MLCC land pattern with no polarity marking anywhere on the board
findings.current_part: Schematic symbol is "Polarized capacitor, small symbol"; the Source field resolves to Kyocera AVX TPSB107K010R0400 - 100 uF, 10 V, case B (EIA 1210 tantalum = 3528-21 metric, 3.50 x 2.80 x 1.90 mm, terminal width W1 2.20 mm, terminal length A 0.80 mm, S min 1.40 mm), ESR max 400 mOhm at 100 kHz, 0.461 A rms at 25 C, DCL max 10 uA (Kyocera AVX TPS series ratings table, 10 V @ 85 C block). The PCB footprint is Bucketmouse:C_1210_3225Metric_Boxed_2: roundrect pads 1.15 x 2.70 mm at +/-1.475 mm, and the F.SilkS artwork is two identical brackets at x = -2.3 and x = +2.3 with no stripe, no chamfer and no "+". I dumped the footprint's six F.SilkS fp_line entries directly from the .kicad_pcb and they are mirror-symmetric.
findings.proposal: Three separable fixes, cheapest first. (a) Add a polarity mark: an F.SilkS stripe or a "+" beside pad 1 of each of CP1/CP2/CP3, plus a pin-1 chamfer on the F.Fab body. Zero cost, zero electrical change. (b) Note that the land is dimensionally fine for the case-B tantalum even though it is named 3225: pads run from 0.825 to 2.075 mm from centre, the tantalum's terminals from 0.95 to 1.75 mm, so there is 0.125 mm inner and 0.325 mm outer overhang and the 2.70 mm pad comfortably covers the 2.20 mm terminal. The only geometric error is the courtyard, which is drawn for a 3.2 x 2.5 mm body and is 0.3 mm undersize in both axes for the 3.5 x 2.8 mm tantalum; the nearest neighbour is 1.0 mm away (CP1/CP2/CP3 are on a 3.8 mm pitch) so nothing collides today. (c) If you would rather not rely on silk, use a non-polar 100 uF 1210 MLCC, which is what the footprint is actually named for - but read the cp1-reverse-bias finding first, because that decision interacts with it.
findings.benefit: No power saving; this is a build-defect guard. Consequence if it is got wrong: CP2 and CP3 sit with a permanent 1.25 V DC forward bias (LM4853 SE outputs are biased at VAUD/2 = 2.5/2 = 1.25 V, with R19/R20 1k to AGND on the load side). Fitted backwards they see 1.25 V continuous reverse, which is 12.5 % of the 10 V rating - above Kyocera AVX's own published limit of "10 % of rated voltage to a maximum of 1 volt at 25 C", and that limit is explicitly stated to apply only to short excursions and "should never be used to determine the maximum reverse voltage under which a capacitor can be used permanently". The failure mode for a reversed MnO2 tantalum is a dead short across a 100 mA-class audio output. On a hobbyist hand-built board with three identical unmarked 1210 pads, this is a when-not-if.
findings.risk: The silk fix has no risk. The courtyard fix is cosmetic unless someone later moves parts near CP1-CP3. Adding a polarity stripe requires a new fab run, so for boards already made the mitigation is documentation only.
findings.verify_reason: Core defect independently CONFIRMED. I resolved the schematic Source field myself (digikey.com/short/332b01qh -> Kyocera AVX TPSB107K010R0400, 100 uF 10 V, ESR 400 mOhm @100 kHz, case '1411 (3528 Metric), 1210'). All three symbols are Device:C_Polarized_Small with Description 'Polarized capacitor, small symbol' in Audio.kicad_sch. I dumped the Bucketmouse:C_1210_3225Metric_Boxed_2 instances out of the fork .kicad_pcb: pads 1.15 x 2.70 at x=+/-1.475, six F.SilkS fp_lines at x=-2.3/+2.3 that are exactly mirror-symmetric, F.Fab a plain rectangle +/-1.6 x +/-1.25 with NO chamfer, no stripe, no '+'. Confirmed. Case B dims confirmed verbatim from the TPS ratings PDF page 1 table (B / 1210 / 3528-21 / 3.50 / 2.80 / 1.90 / W1 2.20 / A 0.80 / S min 1.40). AVX reverse-voltage guideline confirmed verbatim in revtant.pdf s2.0: '10% of rated voltage to a maximum of 1 volt at 25 degC ... These guidelines apply for short excursions and should never be used to determine the maximum reverse voltage under which a capacitor can be used permanently.' LM4853 half-supply SE bias confirmed in a freshly fetched TI PDF. Positions confirmed: CP3 (106.2,-19.3), CP1 (106.2,-23.1), CP2 (106.2,-26.9) = 3.8 mm pitch, 1.0 mm body-to-body. TWO STATED NUMBERS ARE WRONG (see correction). Neither changes the conclusion, so REVISED rather than CONFIRMED.
findings.correction: (1) Pad extents are wrong. 1.475 +/- 1.15/2 gives copper from 0.900 to 2.050 mm from centre, not '0.825 to 2.075'. Against the case-B terminal at 0.95-1.75 mm that is 0.05 mm inner overhang (not 0.125) and 0.30 mm outer overhang (not 0.325). The conclusion that the land is dimensionally fine for the tantalum still holds, but the inner margin is 0.05 mm, i.e. essentially zero, not the comfortable figure quoted. (2) The courtyard claim is backwards. F.CrtYd is +/-2.3 x +/-1.6 = 4.6 x 3.2 mm, which is LARGER than the 3.5 x 2.8 mm (max 3.7 x 3.0 mm) tantalum in both axes - it is not 0.3 mm undersize and needs no fix. What is drawn for a 3.2 x 2.5 mm body is the F.Fab outline, a documentation layer with no clearance meaning. Delete fix (b)'s courtyard half; keep only the silk/pin-1 half. (3) The cited 0.461 A rms figure is taken from the 6.3 V ratings row; the 10 V/400 mOhm case-B row did not extract from the PDF. It happens to be right (case B P_max is 85 mW, so 400 mOhm always gives 0.461 A) but it is not the number the cited block shows.

findings.title: CP1 is a polarized tantalum carrying bidirectional AC with zero DC bias - the speaker BTL output reverse-biases it past AVX's own 1 V limit
findings.current_part: CP1 = TPSB107K010R0400, 100 uF 10 V case-B MnO2 tantalum, ESR max 400 mOhm at 100 kHz. Topology from the netlist: U6 (LM4853) pin BTL+ -> CP1.1 -> CP1.2 = SP1.2; SP1.1 -> U6 LOUT/BTL-. So CP1 sits in series with the 8 Ohm AGB speaker inside the bridge. The LM4853 datasheet states plainly that "Since the differential outputs, BTL OUT- and BTL OUT+, are biased at half-supply, no net DC voltage exists across the load. This eliminates the need for the output coupling capacitor that a single supply, single-ended amplifier configuration requires." So CP1 has 0 V DC across it by design, and the whole signal swing appears across it as bidirectional AC. Speaker impedance 8 Ohm (replacement-part specs for the 23 mm AGB/GBC speaker, distributor data, not a Nintendo datasheet - treat as verified-by-distributor).
findings.proposal: Replace CP1 (only) with a non-polar 100 uF 1210 X5R/X7R MLCC of >= 10 V rating on the identical land - the footprint is literally named C_1210_3225Metric, so this is the part the pads were drawn for and it is a drop-in with no board change. Leave CP2/CP3 as tantalums: they have a proper 1.25 V forward DC bias and are correctly applied. If you prefer to keep a tantalum at CP1, the alternative is to accept the exposure and document it; raising the voltage rating does NOT help, because AVX's guideline caps reverse voltage at 1 V absolute regardless of rating.
findings.benefit: Reliability, plus about 1-2.5 mW of recovered audio power at loud volume. Reverse-voltage arithmetic: |Zc| of 100 uF is 31.8 Ohm at 50 Hz, 15.9 Ohm at 100 Hz, 8.0 Ohm at 200 Hz, 4.0 Ohm at 400 Hz. The fraction of the amplifier's output that appears across CP1 is |Zc|/|8 + Zc| = 0.97, 0.89, 0.71 and 0.45 respectively. The LM4853 on a 2.5 V rail can swing roughly 1.5 Vrms differential before clipping, so a loud 100 Hz passage puts ~1.3 Vrms = 1.9 Vpk across CP1, and the negative half-cycle reverse-biases it to ~1.9 V - about twice AVX's "10 % of rated to a maximum of 1 volt at 25 C" figure. Even a modest 1.0 Vrms at 200 Hz reaches 0.71 Vrms = 1.0 Vpk, exactly at the limit. Power side: at 50 mW into the speaker, Irms = sqrt(0.05/8) = 79 mA, so CP1's 400 mOhm ESR burns 0.079^2 x 0.4 = 2.5 mW; a 100 uF MLCC at roughly 5 mOhm recovers essentially all of that, and also raises delivered power by 20*log10(8.4/8.25) = 0.16 dB. At 20 mW output the recovery is 1.0 mW.
findings.risk: Two real downsides to the MLCC. (1) Class-II ceramic has an AC voltage coefficient, so a 1-2 V swing across it modulates its own capacitance and produces low-order distortion in exactly the band where the cap is doing work (below ~400 Hz). (2) MLCCs are piezoelectric and a 3225 part carrying 80 mA of audio current can sing audibly. Against that, the high-pass corner with 8 Ohm + 0.4 Ohm ESR is 189 Hz (1/(2*pi*8.4*100e-6)), and TI's own note is that portable speakers "have little ability to reproduce signals below 150 Hz" - so the frequency region where the ceramic misbehaves is the region the speaker cannot reproduce anyway. The counter-risk of doing nothing is a slow-degrading tantalum in a hand-built console. Confidence is not higher because AVX's reverse-voltage guideline is explicitly written for DC excursions, and audio half-cycles are the mildest kind of excursion; the practical failure rate on existing AGBM builds is unknown to me.
findings.verify_reason: Reliability half survives; power half is refuted outright. VERIFIED: topology from the fork netlist (CP1.1=Net-(U6-BTL+), CP1.2=Net-(CP1-Pad2)=SP1.2; SP1.1=Net-(U6-LOUT/BTL-)) so CP1 really is inside the bridge with no DC path to anything, i.e. 0 V DC bias by construction. TI LM4853 PDF (freshly fetched, not the finding's citation) states verbatim 'the differential outputs, BTL OUT- and BTL OUT+, are biased at half-supply, no net DC voltage exists across the load'. AVX revtant.pdf confirms the 1 V/25 degC guideline and explicitly recommends back-to-back pairs where reverse excursions are unavoidable. Zc arithmetic all recomputed and correct (31.83/15.92/7.96/3.98 ohm; divider fractions 0.970/0.893/0.705/0.446). REFUTED - the power benefit. (a) The assumed operating point is impossible on this board: MouseBiteLabs measures the whole audio subsystem at 50-100 mW at max volume, and TI gives IDD 1.8 mA at 2.7 V. Working the class-B relation P_supply = (2/pi)*VDD*Ipk + Pq at VAUD=2.5 V with 75-100 mW available gives Ipk = 44-60 mA and P_out = 8-15 mW into 8 ohm, not the 50 mW assumed. CP1's ESR dissipation at the real ceiling is Ipk^2*ESR/2 = 0.06^2*0.4/2 = 0.72 mW, not 2.5 mW. (b) More fundamentally, none of it is recoverable. For a class-AB output stage the supply power is set by peak output CURRENT (P_supply = 2*VDD*Ipk/pi), not by the series impedance. At constant acoustic output Ipk is fixed, so removing 0.4 ohm of ESR moves that dissipation from the capacitor into the amplifier die and leaves battery draw unchanged. The correct saving is 0 mW, not 1 mW. (c) The '0.16 dB' figure uses an unexplained 8.25 ohm and applies 20*log10 to an impedance ratio; the delivered-power change at constant drive voltage is (8.4/8.005)^2 = 0.42 dB. (d) The proposal calls the MLCC 'a drop-in with no board change' without checking height: the only stocked 100 uF 1210 X5R at >=10 V (Murata GRM32ER61A107ME20K) is 3.2 x 2.5 x 2.5 mm, i.e. 2.5 mm tall against the tantalum's 1.90 mm case-B height - 0.6 mm taller inside a GBA shell, unverified.
findings.correction: Keep the reliability finding, drop the power claim to 0 mW. Reverse-voltage exposure recomputed at the real ceiling (Ipk ~60 mA): ~0.95 V peak reverse at 100 Hz, ~1.9 V peak at 50 Hz - so the finding's 1.9 V number is roughly right by accident, arrived at from an unreachable output level. Rate the MLCC swap as 'drop-in on the land, mechanical height check required (2.5 mm vs 1.90 mm)', not 'no board change'. The finding also omits the cheapest option: because the datasheet says the BTL configuration needs no output coupling capacitor at all, and because SE-mode muting is done by A2 going high-impedance rather than by CP1, a 0-ohm 1210 link is a genuine zero-cost alternative that removes both the polarized-part hazard and the 189 Hz speaker high-pass. Its cost is losing DC-fault protection for the speaker; flag, do not assume.

findings.title: The SRAM has no decoupling capacitor within 7 mm of any VDD2 pin, and ECO-5 made it worse
findings.current_part: VDD2 pads on U2 and their nearest VDD2 capacitor, computed from the fork board file: pin 12 (81.31, -58.05) -> C46 (1 uF) at 9.9 mm; pin 16 (81.31, -56.05) -> C46 at 8.0 mm; pin 37, stock outer column (95.10, -58.05) -> C8 (0.1 uF) at 9.9 mm; pin 37, CY62157 third column (100.31, -58.05) -> C8 at 7.1 mm. For comparison the CPU is properly served: U1 pin 44 has C15 at 2.6 mm and C46 at 4.5 mm, pin 65 has C16 at 2.4 mm and C48 at 3.6 mm, pins 115/117 have C45/C47 at 2.5-2.7 mm and C52/C53 at 3.1-3.7 mm. ECO-5 moved C8 from (100.8, -59.3) - 5.7 mm from the stock pin 37 - to (103.0, -64.9), which is 7.1 mm from the pad a CY62157 actually lands on. The fork's own README also records that "Five GND stitching vias and eleven plane segments under the new body were removed (re-stitch before fab)", so the return path under U2 is currently degraded as well.
findings.proposal: Add two 0603 caps on B.Cu directly under the SRAM, where the layer is empty: one 0.1 uF (C0603C104K5RACTU, same as C8) at roughly (82.0, -56.0) to serve pins 12/16, and one 0.1 uF at roughly (94.0, -55.5) to serve pin 37. Both locations are clear of every existing B.Cu footprint in that region (nearest are RA1 ending at y = -58.5, R35 at -58.5, R65 and C72 at -57.3, U14 at -56.5) and both sit outside the B.Cu cartridge rule area, which forbids pads only for y between -54.2 and -32.2. Optionally move C8 back toward pin 37 as well. Route each cap's GND pad to In1.Cu with its own via next to the pad, not through a shared stub. Then finish the ECO-5 re-stitching the README already calls for.
findings.benefit: No power saving - this is a signal-integrity fix. The size of the problem: at 8-10 mm the loop from an SRAM VCC pin to the nearest cap is roughly 16-20 mm of go-and-return path. Using the usual ~1 nH/mm rule of thumb for a trace over a nearby plane (this is an engineering estimate, not a datasheet number) that is 15-20 nH, whose impedance at 100 MHz is 9-13 Ohm. Bringing a cap to 2 mm cuts that by roughly a factor of four. What saves the current board from this being a fault rather than a weakness is that VDD2 is a plane, not a trace: the In2.Cu VDD2 zone spans x 16.8-101.8, y -63.2 to -31.6 and therefore covers every U2 VDD2 pad, sitting over a solid In1.Cu ground plane. That plane pair is what is actually doing the high-frequency work today. With the ClockxControl at 1.75x the SRAM is cycled at 7.34 MHz instead of 4.19 MHz, so edge-rate current demand rises by the same factor and the margin this design has been getting away with shrinks proportionally.
findings.risk: Low. Two 0603 caps and two vias. The only real risk is putting them where they foul the CY62157 body or the re-poured planes, so they must be placed and DRC'd in KiCad rather than trusted from my coordinates - I checked footprint bounding boxes and the B.Cu rule area, not the finished copper. Note also that if you populate an original salvaged GBA RAM instead of the CY62157, pin 37 sits at x = 95.10 and the second cap should move accordingly (or be placed midway to serve both).
findings.verify_reason: I recomputed every distance from the fork board file independently (pad-level, all footprint rotations applied) and every number matches to 0.02 mm. U2 VDD2 pads: pin 12 (81.31,-58.05) nearest VDD2 cap C46 at 9.92 mm (finding 9.9); pin 16 (81.31,-56.05) C46 at 8.01 mm (finding 8.0); pin 37 stock-column pad (95.10,-58.05) C8 at 9.88 mm (finding 9.9); pin 37 CY62157 third-column pad (100.31,-58.05) C8 at 7.11 mm (finding 7.1). CPU for contrast: pin 44 -> C15 2.62 mm / C46 4.51 mm; pin 65 -> C16 2.39 / C48 3.58; pins 115/117 -> C45/C47 2.47-3.04 mm. ECO-5 move confirmed by diffing the stock board: C8 was at (100.8,-59.3), now (103.0,-64.9); against the stock pin-37 pad that is 5.7 mm before and 9.9 mm after, so ECO-5 did make it worse on both SRAM variants. README quote confirmed verbatim ('Five GND stitching vias and eleven plane segments under the new body were removed (re-stitch before fab)'). Plane claims confirmed from the zone table: In1.Cu is a full GND pour, the In2.Cu VDD2 zone spans x 16.80-101.80, y -63.25 to -31.62 and therefore covers all five U2 VDD2 pads (the outermost, x=100.31, with 1.5 mm to spare). The B.Cu cartridge rule area is exactly x 33.10-105.10, y -54.20 to -32.20, so the two proposed B.Cu locations at y=-56.0 and -55.5 are outside it - though the second clears the boundary by only ~0.4 mm once the 0603 body is drawn, which is why the finding is right to insist on a KiCad DRC. The 1 nH/mm and mounting-inductance figures are explicitly labelled as engineering estimates, which is the correct treatment. Only defect: the 'sources' line cites the NCV8164 datasheet, which has nothing to do with this finding - a citation-hygiene slip, not a factual error.

findings.title: The ClockxControl taps VDD3 at cartridge pad S1, 43.5 mm from the nearest bypass capacitor and 68 mm from its load switch
findings.current_part: Verified from the fork netlist: P1 pad S1 = net VDD3, at (96.90, -35.20) on F.Cu. Nearest VDD3 capacitor is C69 (1 uF) at 43.5 mm; then C49 (1 uF) at 44.6 mm and C5 (0.1 uF) at 44.8 mm. The rail's source, U18 (TPS22917 load switch), is at (29.47, -27.30) on B.Cu - 68 mm away. Total VDD3 decoupling on the whole board after derating is 3 x 1 uF at 0.875 uF each plus 4 x 0.1 uF at 0.100 uF each = 3.03 uF, and none of it is anywhere near the tap. VDD3 does have an In2.Cu plane pour (x 23.6-98.1, y -52.2 to -26.6) which reaches S1 with about 1.2 mm to spare in x.
findings.proposal: Add a 1 uF 16 V X7R 0603 (KEMET C0603C105K4RACTU - already on the BOM as C45-C51 etc., so no new line item) and a 0.1 uF 50 V X7R 0603 (C0603C104K5RACTU, also already on the BOM) on F.Cu at roughly (100.5, -37.0), about 4 mm from S1. That location is clear of P1's courtyard (which ends at x = 97.65), clear of R37 (98.37 to 99.83 in x, -34.48 to -31.52 in y) and - importantly - outside the ECO-6 ClockxControl mezzanine window, which occupies x 82.625-101.275, y -50.950 to -38.950 on F.Cu. B.Cu is not available there: the cartridge rule area forbids pads for x 33.1-105.1, y -54.2 to -32.2.
findings.benefit: No measurable power saving; the argument is clock jitter, not droop. The module contains the oscillator that drives the CPU's XIN, so ripple and noise on its 3.3 V supply translate directly into period jitter on a 7.34 MHz clock feeding a salvaged CPU that was specified for 4.194 MHz - the one part of this build with the least characterisation margin. Droop is genuinely not the concern: the module's ~12 mA over a plane pair spanning 43 mm is maybe a few nH of spreading inductance, and 12 mA through that is nothing. The concern is that there is currently zero local charge reservoir for whatever the module's internal switching does, and the fix costs two 0603s of parts already on the BOM.
findings.risk: Very low electrically. The practical risk is mechanical: the area around P1's S1 pad is congested and the ClockxControl mezzanine window is immediately below it, so the placement must be confirmed in KiCad against the mezzanine keepout and the cart-slot shell. My coordinates come from footprint bounding boxes, not from routed copper.
findings.verify_reason: Every measurement checks out; the proposal has a defect the finding did not catch. VERIFIED by my own pad-level recomputation: P1 pad S1 is net VDD3 at exactly (96.90,-35.20) on F.Cu; nearest VDD3 cap pad is C69 at 43.48 mm (finding 43.5), then C49 at 44.57 (44.6) and C5 at 44.83 (44.8); U18 (B.Cu, 29.474,-27.30) is 67.9 mm away (finding 68). VDD3 net has exactly 3 x 1 uF (C49,C50,C69) and 4 x 0.1 uF (C5,C34,C39,C43); derated total 3*0.875 + 4*0.100 = 3.025 uF, matching 3.03. The In2.Cu VDD3 zone bounding box is x 23.60-98.10, y -52.19 to -26.60 as stated, and I went further and ran a point-in-polygon test on the actual FILLED polygon: (96.9,-35.2) IS inside the poured VDD3 copper, so the plane genuinely reaches S1. R37 extents and the ECO-6 window clearance also check out, and no F.Cu footprint sits within 4 mm of (100.5,-37.0). DEFECT: the same point-in-polygon test says (100.5,-37.0) is NOT inside the VDD3 In2.Cu pour - the pour stops at x~98.1. So the proposed caps cannot drop straight onto the plane through a via; they need a routed VDD3 trace of ~2.5-4 mm back to S1 or the plane edge. That is still far better than 43 mm, but it is not the plane-stitched reservoir the write-up implies.
findings.correction: Rate the placement as 'trace-connected, not plane-connected': at x=100.5 the cap sits outside the In2.Cu VDD3 pour (which ends at x=98.1), so route a short wide VDD3 trace to S1 and give the GND pad its own via to In1.Cu. If the mezzanine and P1 courtyard allow, x<=98 keeps the cap over the pour. Also soften the premise: the write-up asserts 'zero local charge reservoir' for the module, but insideGadgets' ClockxControl is an assembled module and its own on-board decoupling was not checked either way - so this is a cheap belt-and-braces measure, not a demonstrated deficiency. Everything else stands.

findings.title: L1/L2 DCR is the only real efficiency lever in this domain - worth 3 mW normally, 6 mW overclocked, 11 mW at max brightness plus overclock
findings.current_part: Taiyo Yuden LSXND3030QKT4R7MNG (previous PN NRS3015T4R7MNGH): 4.7 uH +/-20 %, DCR 0.120 Ohm typ / 0.144 Ohm max, Isat 1.02 A at dL = 30 %, Itemp 1.04 A at dT = 40 C, body 3.0 x 3.0 x 1.5 mm max, terminal e = 0.9 +/-0.2 mm, f = 1.9 +/-0.2 mm. The KiCad footprint is misleadingly named L_Taiyo-Yuden_NR-20xx_HandSoldering but its pads are 1.65 x 2.00 mm on a 2.35 mm pitch, i.e. copper from 0.35 to 1.55 mm from centre - which correctly captures the 3030 part's terminals at 0.6 to 1.5 mm with sensible overhang. So the land is right and only the library name is wrong.
findings.proposal: Wurth WE-MAPI 74438356047: 4.7 uH +/-20 %, DCR 63 mOhm typ / 76 mOhm max, Isat(30 %) 5.75 A typ, IRP,40K 4 A, body 4.1 x 4.1 x 2.1 mm, recommended land 1.39 mm pads on a 3.7 mm span with a 3.35 mm pad height. Only L2 needs it (ch2 carries the CPU/SRAM/logic/audio load and takes all the overclock current); L1 can stay. I checked the obvious same-footprint alternatives and they are all worse: Taiyo Yuden LSDND3030MKT4R7MM (metal composite, 3.0 x 3.0 x 1.2 mm, identical e/f terminals) is 0.228 Ohm typ / 0.263 max, and LCDND3030KKT4R7MM (3.0 x 3.0 x 1.0 mm) is 0.300 typ / 0.345 max. There is no drop-in improvement on the existing land - the fitted part is already the best of the family.
findings.benefit: P = DCR x (I_L1^2 + I_L2^2), using typical DCR. At 792 mW in use (I_L1 = 132 mA, I_L2 = 198 mA): 0.120 x (0.01742 + 0.03920) = 6.8 mW today, 0.063 x same = 3.6 mW with the MAPI, saving 3.2 mW. With the overclock (I_L2 = 299 mA): 0.120 x (0.01742 + 0.08940) = 12.8 mW today vs 6.7 mW, saving 6.1 mW. At the Hispeedido max-brightness point 1175 mW plus overclock (I_L1 = 220 mA, I_L2 = 371 mA): 0.120 x (0.04862 + 0.13727) = 22.3 mW today vs 11.7 mW, saving 10.6 mW. Using max DCR instead of typ the numbers become 8.2/15.4/26.8 mW today, saving up to 12.6 mW. Set against a 792-1420 mW overclocked in-use budget that is 0.4 % to 0.8 % of system power - real, but it will not show up on a battery-life graph. Note the overclock by itself adds 6 mW of inductor loss (12.8 - 6.8) at the 792 mW point purely from the extra 101 mA on L2.
findings.risk: Three separate problems, all real. (1) It does not fit on the current layout: a 4.1 x 4.1 mm body centred on L2 (29.5, -34.8) sweeps a courtyard of roughly x 27.25-31.75, y -37.05 to -32.55, which collides with C42 (30.77-32.73, -39.90 to -36.50); doing the same at L1 (29.5, -45) collides with C21 and grazes U11. Both bulk output caps would have to move. (2) Height goes from 1.5 mm to 2.1 mm on B.Cu, which faces the cart/battery side of a GBA shell - I have no verified clearance figure and this must be measured on a real shell before committing. (3) The 4.7 uH value must be kept: the LTC3527 datasheet says 3.3-4.7 uH suits 1.2 MHz operation and that larger inductance slightly raises maximum output current, and channel 2's headroom is already the thin one (the datasheet's Maximum Output Current vs VIN curve for converter 2 reads roughly 300 mA at VIN = 2.4 V, VOUT = 3.3 V, against my estimated ~150 mA VOUT3 load with the overclock - fine at 2.4 V, less comfortable at the 1.8 V end of discharge). Verdict: real but marginal; I would take the sram and clockxcontrol fixes first and only do this if the board is being respun anyway.
findings.verify_reason: Parts and part data all CONFIRMED from primary sources I fetched myself. Taiyo Yuden TYCOMPAS page for LSXND3030QKT4R7MNG: 4.7 uH +/-20%, DCR 0.12 ohm typ / 0.144 max, Isat 1.02 A (dL=30%), Itemp 1.04 A (dT=40 K), 3.0+/-0.1 x 3.0+/-0.1 x 1.5 max, e=0.9+/-0.2, f=1.9+/-0.2 - every number as stated. DigiKey confirms DCR 144 mOhm max / Isat 1.02 A / 3030. Wurth 74438356047 datasheet (fetched and text-extracted): 4.7 uH +/-20%, RDC 63 mOhm typ / 76 max, Isat30% 5.75 A typ, IRP,40K 4 A, 4.1 x 4.1 x 2.1 max, recommended land 1.39 x 3.35 pads on a 3.7 mm span - every number as stated. LTC3527 datasheet quote confirmed verbatim: 'Inductor values between 3.3uH and 4.7uH are suitable for most 1.2MHz applications. Larger values of inductance will allow slightly greater output current capability (and lower the Burst Mode threshold)'. Collision claims verified from footprint geometry: a 4.1 x 4.1 body on L2 (29.5,-34.8) overlaps C42 (30.77-32.73, -39.90 to -36.50) by ~0.78 x 0.35 mm, and the same at L1 against C21 - real, as stated. BUT THE BENEFIT ARITHMETIC CONTRADICTS THE PROPOSAL, which is why this is REVISED not CONFIRMED.
findings.correction: (1) The headline saving is inflated ~45%. The proposal says 'Only L2 needs it ... L1 can stay', but every benefit line multiplies the NEW 63 mOhm across BOTH inductor currents: 0.063*(I_L1^2 + I_L2^2). For an L2-only swap the saving is (0.120-0.063)*I_L2^2. Redone on the finding's own current assumptions: at 792 mW (I_L2=198 mA) 0.057*0.03920 = 2.23 mW, not 3.2; overclocked (299 mA) 0.057*0.08940 = 5.10 mW, not 6.1; at 1175 mW + overclock (371 mA) 0.057*0.13727 = 7.82 mW, not 10.6. Claim 2.2 mW / 5.1 mW overclocked. (2) The footprint pad extent is wrong. Pads are 1.65 x 2.00 mm at x=+/-1.175, so copper runs 0.35 to 2.050 mm from centre, not 'to 1.55'. Total land span is 4.0 mm, wider than the 3.0 mm body - it is a hand-solder land with a large outer toe, which is why the outer overhang is 0.55 mm, not the small figure implied. (3) 'The land is right and only the library name is wrong' is not quite true: the footprint's F.CrtYd is +/-2.25 x +/-1.30 mm and its F.Fab body is 2.0 x 2.0 mm, both drawn for the NR-20xx part it is named after. For the fitted 3.0 x 3.0 mm body the courtyard is 0.2 mm undersize per side in y, so DRC will not catch a neighbour placed against it. The copper land is fine; the courtyard is not. (4) The market survey is thin - it only walks the Taiyo Yuden 3030 family. Coilcraft XGL3520-472 (4.7 uH, 72.6 mOhm max, 3.5 x 3.5 x 2.0 mm) is a much smaller intrusion than the 4020 MAPI, though DigiKey lists it as no longer available and even 3.5 mm still just grazes C42, so the 'needs a PCB revision' verdict stands either way.

findings.title: C21 loses 51 % of its capacitance at 5.014 V and is the sole bulk cap on the rail that feeds the backlight - still legal, but it is the tightest node on the board
findings.current_part: C21 = Murata GRM21BR61E226ME44L, 22 uF +/-20 % 25 V X5R 0805, body 2.0 x 1.25 x 1.25 mm, cap change rate +/-15 % over -55 to +85 C. Murata's own DC-bias chart, digitised: -51.5 % at 5.014 V, giving 10.66 uF. Add the tolerance and the X5R temperature band and the worst case is 22 x 0.80 x 0.485 x 0.85 = 7.25 uF. The only other capacitor on VOUT5 is C72, 0.1 uF, which contributes 0.099 uF. So the rail has 10.76 uF effective against 22.1 uF nominal, i.e. 49 %.
findings.proposal: No change required. If you are respinning the board anyway, add a second 22 uF 0805 land in parallel with C21 on B.Cu near U5 pin 5 (VOUT1). Do not try to solve this with a bigger nominal value in the same 0805: I could not obtain a verified DC-bias curve for the obvious candidate (Murata GRM21BR60J476ME15L, 47 uF 6.3 V X5R 0805), and 6.3 V-rated dielectric at a 5.0 V bias is exactly the case where the derating is worst, so substituting it on faith would be a mistake. Marked unverified deliberately.
findings.benefit: No power saving. The reason to know this number: VOUT5 is the rail that carries the LCD analog supply VSHA (FFC pin 34, via U11) and therefore the brightness-dependent load - the 568-to-1175 mW swing on a Hispeedido panel is this rail. It is also the rail with the least bulk capacitance in effective terms (10.8 uF, versus 28.0 uF on VOUT3), and if the screen kit PWM-dims the backlight, VOUT5 sees the resulting load steps. The LTC3527 is specified as stable with COUT >= 4.7 uF and the datasheet recommends 4.7-10 uF with "larger values up to 22 uF" for lower ripple and better transient response, so at 10.7 uF typical and 7.25 uF worst case the rail is compliant with margin - it just has far less margin than the 22 uF marking suggests. Burst-mode ripple, which the datasheet gives as typically 1 % p-p, is also already mitigated by C40, the 15 pF C0G feed-forward cap the datasheet asks for.
findings.risk: None from leaving it alone. Adding a parallel 22 uF costs board area on a crowded B.Cu and would raise the load current at which channel 1 leaves Burst Mode (the datasheet warns that "larger output capacitor values may cause this transition to occur at lighter loads"), which would slightly hurt idle efficiency on the 5 V channel. On balance, leave it.
findings.verify_reason: I re-derived the central number independently rather than trusting the digitisation. digikey.com/short/3mhhrd2f resolves to Murata GRM21BR61E226ME44L, 22 uF +/-20% 25 V X5R 0805. The Murata datasheet (farnell 1747471) page 1 gives L 2.0+/-0.2, W 1.25+/-0.2, T 1.25+/-0.2 mm and 'Capacitance change rate +/-15.0%' over -55 to +85 degC - exactly as stated. I rendered the DC-bias chart on page 2 at 500 dpi, located the gridlines programmatically and read the blue trace: -50.8% at 5.014 V, giving 10.83 uF, against the finding's -51.5% / 10.66 uF. Agreement to within digitisation error. Worst-case stack 22*0.80*0.485*0.85 = 7.26 uF recomputed correctly. C72 is the only other VOUT5 capacitor (net dump: VOUT5 carries C21, C72 and C40, and C40 is the 15 pF FB1 feed-forward, not bulk), and 0.1 uF at 5 V is 0.099 uF, so 10.76 uF against 22.1 uF nominal = 49%. Correct. LTC3527 quotes all confirmed verbatim: '4.7uF to 10uF output capacitor is sufficient ... Larger values up to 22uF may be used', 'designed to be stable with output capacitor values of 4.7uF or greater', 'Burst Mode output voltage ripple, which is typically 1% peak-to-peak', and 15 pF as the recommended feed-forward value. Recommendation (leave it alone) stands. Two nits that do not change the verdict: the risk paragraph says adding capacitance would 'raise the load current at which channel 1 leaves Burst Mode', which is the opposite of the datasheet sentence it quotes (larger COUT makes the exit happen at LIGHTER loads) - the conclusion drawn is nevertheless the right one; and the whole Burst Mode concern is moot anyway, because the datasheet requires BOTH outputs to be lightly loaded and channel 2 is not (see my verdict on cout-cannot-buy-burst-mode). The claim that VOUT5/VSHA carries the brightness-dependent load is an inference from the net map, not a measurement, and is correctly hedged.

findings.title: VDD2 decoupling does NOT need strengthening at the CPU for 7.34 MHz - the numbers say it has an order of magnitude of margin
findings.current_part: Inventory from the net map: C60 10 uF 0603 (25 V X5R) at (18.4, -33.8) on B.Cu, 3.5 mm from U8 - this is the LDO's output capacitor, not CPU decoupling, and it is 33 mm from the CPU. Local to U1: C45/C46/C47/C48 1 uF 16 V X7R and C8/C15/C16/C52/C53 0.1 uF 50 V X7R. After derating at 2.5 V: 7.39 + 4 x 0.968 + 5 x 0.1007 = 11.76 uF total, of which 4.37 uF is local to the CPU. VDD2 is a plane on In2.Cu (zone x 16.8-101.8, y -63.2 to -31.6) over a solid In1.Cu ground plane. NCV8164 requires COUT >= 1 uF ceramic with no minimum ESR, Iq 30 uA typ, dropout 125 mV typ at 300 mA for the 2.5 V variant, current limit 350 mA min.
findings.proposal: Change nothing at U1. Three independent checks all clear comfortably. (1) Target impedance: allow 5 % ripple on 2.5 V = 125 mV; taking my estimated 117 mA of CPU dynamic current at 7.34 MHz and a 50 % step, Ztarget = 0.125/0.058 = 2.15 Ohm. (2) Charge transfer per clock: Q = 0.117 A / 7.34 MHz = 15.9 nC; against the 4.37 uF of local effective capacitance that is dV = 3.6 mV per cycle, 35x under budget. (3) High-frequency impedance: at an estimated 1.5-2.5 nH of mounting-plus-via loop inductance per 0603 (engineering estimate, not a datasheet figure), nine caps in parallel give ~0.22 nH, so |Z| at 200 MHz = 2*pi*2e8*0.22e-9 = 0.28 Ohm, still 7x under the 2.15 Ohm target. The physical placement backs this up: every one of U1's four VDD2 pins has a 0.1 uF within 2.4-3.7 mm and a 1 uF within 2.5-4.5 mm.
findings.benefit: No power saving. The value of this finding is negative-result value: the obvious instinct with a 1.75x overclock is to pile capacitance onto VDD2, and the arithmetic says that would be wasted board area and wasted money. The one place the network genuinely IS weak is the SRAM, which is a separate finding. Worth adding: because U8 is an LDO, every milliamp the overclock adds to VDD2 also comes out of VOUT3 and burns (3.336 - 2.500) = 0.836 V in U8 - 50 mA of extra core current costs 42 mW of pure heat in a SOT-23-5. That is a bigger lever than anything in my domain, but it is an LDO/topology question, not a passives question.
findings.risk: The mounting-inductance figure is an estimate, so the 200 MHz impedance number is indicative rather than measured. If a build shows instability at 1.75x, the thing to instrument is VDD2 at TP18 with a short-ground-spring probe before adding capacitors - the likely culprits are the SRAM's missing local cap and the ECO-5 plane damage, not the CPU decoupling count. Also note U8's 350 mA minimum current limit: my estimated 117 mA of core current at 1.75x leaves headroom, but that estimate is derived from insideGadgets' system-level figure, not measured.
findings.verify_reason: Conclusion (change nothing at U1) survives, and I verified the inputs rather than the prose. NCV8164 datasheet: dropout for the 2.5 V variant in TSOP-5 is 125 mV typ / 200 mV max at 300 mA; output current limit 350 mA min / 560 typ; IQ 30 uA typ / 40 max; 'Stable with a 1 uF Small Case Size Ceramic Capacitors' - all four numbers exactly as stated. Derated capacitance values re-derived from my own 500 dpi digitisations of the Murata charts: 10 uF 25 V 0603 at 2.5 V = 7.36 uF (finding 7.39); 1 uF 16 V X7R 0603 at 2.5 V = 0.964 uF (finding 0.968). Sum 7.36 + 4*0.964 + 5*0.1007 = 11.72 uF against the stated 11.76. Arithmetic all reproduces: Ztarget 0.125/0.058 = 2.16 ohm; Q = 0.117/7.34e6 = 15.9 nC and dV = 3.65 mV, 34x under budget; nine 0603s at 2 nH give 0.22 nH and 0.28 ohm at 200 MHz, 7.7x under target. Placement claims re-measured pad-to-pad and confirmed (every U1 VDD2 pin has a 0.1 uF at 2.39-3.75 mm and a 1 uF at 2.47-4.51 mm). TWO CAVEATS worth recording, neither overturning the finding. (1) The 117 mA CPU-core estimate does not reconcile with the measured envelope: 117 mA at 2.5 V is 293 mW on VDD2 alone, which through U8's LDO drop and the boost is ~440 mW at the battery - more than the 410 mW measured minimum for the WHOLE console. It is therefore a substantial overestimate. That is safe here (it makes both the target-impedance check and the U8 current-limit check conservative) but the number should be labelled as an upper bound, not an estimate. (2) The '4.37 uF local to the CPU' figure counts C8, which after ECO-5 sits at (103.0,-64.9), more than 20 mm from the CPU and 7 mm from the SRAM - it contributes nothing at U1. Local total is 4.28 uF over eight caps; 200 MHz impedance becomes 0.31 ohm. Immaterial to the conclusion. The observation that 50 mA of extra core current costs (3.336-2.500)*0.050 = 41.8 mW of pure heat in U8 is arithmetically correct and is the most valuable sentence in the finding.

findings.title: EM1/EM2/EM3/EM7 and RA1 sit on signal and accessory nets that carry essentially zero DC - their I2R loss is 0 mW
findings.current_part: EM1/EM2 = TDK ACM2520-801-3P-T002, 3-line common-mode choke, 800 Ohm at 100 MHz, rated current 150 mA, DC resistance 1.6 Ohm, SMD-6P 2.5 x 2.0 mm. EM3/EM7 = Bourns MH1608-601Y, 600 Ohm at 100 MHz +/-25 %, DC resistance 200 mOhm max, rated current 1 A, 0603 (1.6 x 0.8 x 0.8 mm). Nets, straight from the board file: EM1 filters /CPU/SO, /CPU/SI and /CPU/LGND; EM2 filters /CPU/SCK, /CPU/SD and /CPU/LGND - all six are AGB link-port serial lines and the link-port ground, each already in series with a 330 Ohm element of RA1. EM3 sits between VDD35 and Net-(P4-VDD35), i.e. it feeds only the link connector's VDD pin - I checked specifically that it is NOT in the cartridge supply path, because P1 pad 1 and pad C1 connect to VDD35 directly, upstream of EM3. EM7 sits between /~RESET and U1H's ~RESET input, a high-impedance logic input.
findings.proposal: Leave all of them alone. There is nothing to win.
findings.benefit: Zero, and that is the finding. With no link cable attached, all five parts carry no DC current at all: 0.144 W/A^2 x 0^2 = 0 mW. Even in the worst realistic case - a link accessory drawing 20 mA from VDD35 - the supply leg through EM3 dissipates 0.020^2 x 0.2 = 0.08 mW and the return leg through one ACM2520 winding dissipates 0.020^2 x 1.6 = 0.64 mW, both only while the accessory is plugged in. EM7 sees at most the 185 uA that R29's 18k pull-up sources into the reset net (3.336/18000), for 0.007 microwatts. RA1's 330 Ohm elements likewise carry only link-port signal current. Against a 170 mW idle and a 410-1175 mW in-use budget this is not a rounding error, it is exactly zero. The one thing worth noting rather than removing: because the ACM2520's third winding carries the link-port ground return at 1.6 Ohm, any future accessory drawing appreciable current through the EXT port would develop a real offset on LGND - 20 mA gives 32 mV. Not a problem for GBA link cables; would be for anything drawing hundreds of mA.
findings.risk: None from leaving them. If anyone were tempted to delete them to save cost, the cost is EMI compliance and ESD robustness on an exposed external connector, for no power benefit whatsoever.
findings.verify_reason: Every part spec and every net claim checks out. TDK ACM2520-801-3P-T002 (LCSC product page): 800 ohm @100 MHz, rated current 150 mA, DC resistance 1.6 ohm, SMD-6P 2.5 x 2.0 mm - as stated. Bourns MH1608-601Y (Newark listing, titled 'FERRITE BEAD, 600 OHM, 25%, 1A, 0603'): 600 ohm +/-25%, DCR 200 mOhm max, 1 A, 0603 1.6 x 0.8 x 0.8 mm - as stated. Net topology re-dumped from the fork board and confirmed: RA1's four 330 ohm elements sit between U1 pins 40/41/42/43 (SC, SD, SI, SO) and the EM1/EM2 windings, all link-port serial lines. The key claim about EM3 is CORRECT and I checked it the same way the finding says it did: the VDD35 net carries P1 pad 1 and P1 pad C1 directly alongside EM3 pad 1, so the cartridge supply is upstream of the bead and only P4 (link connector) sits behind it. EM7 lies between /~RESET and U1 pin 125's ~RESET input. Conclusion (zero I2R, leave everything alone) is right, and the LGND offset note (20 mA x 1.6 ohm = 32 mV) is correct arithmetic. Two cosmetic slips that do not change anything: the constant '0.144 W/A^2' used in the first calculation is L1/L2's max DCR, not any choke's; and EM7 does not carry R29's 185 uA pull-up current at all (that current sinks into U5's PGOOD1 open drain), it carries only the CPU's input leakage - the answer is even closer to zero than claimed.

findings.title: CP2/CP3 audio coupling: a 250 mOhm drop-in exists, but the honest answer on audible improvement is no - except with 16 Ohm earbuds
findings.current_part: CP2/CP3 = TPSB107K010R0400, 100 uF 10 V case-B tantalum, ESR max 400 mOhm at 100 kHz, DCL max 10 uA. Topology: CP2 from U6 LOUT/BTL- to the jack's left contact with R20 1k to AGND; CP3 from U6 ROUT to the jack's right contact with R19 1k to AGND. DC bias across each is VAUD/2 = 1.25 V in the correct polarity, i.e. 12.5 % of rating - a properly applied polarized cap with plenty of margin, and crucially with NO meaningful DC-bias capacitance loss, which is the one place a tantalum beats a 1210 MLCC outright.
findings.proposal: If you want the lowest-ESR drop-in on the identical land, Kyocera AVX's TPS table lists TPSB107*006#0250 - case B, 100 uF, 6.3 V, ESR max 250 mOhm, 0.583 A rms at 25 C. 6.3 V is still 5x the 1.25 V applied bias, so the derating in voltage rating is safe here (it is NOT safe for CP1, which has zero DC bias - see cp1-reverse-bias-btl). Do not substitute a 100 uF MLCC at CP2/CP3: unlike CP1, these have a real DC bias, so a 6.3 V or 10 V 1210 X5R would lose a large fraction of its capacitance at 1.25 V and push the high-pass corner the wrong way.
findings.benefit: Be honest: essentially nothing audible. ESR path: 400 mOhm in series with a 32 Ohm headphone is 1.2 % of the load, worth 20*log10(32.4/32.25) = 0.04 dB. Going to 250 mOhm changes that to 0.02 dB. Nobody hears this. High-pass corner is the only thing that matters, and it is set by the capacitance, not the dielectric: the load is the headphone in parallel with R19/R20 1k, so 32 Ohm || 1k = 31.0 Ohm gives f(-3 dB) = 1/(2*pi*31.0*100e-6) = 51.3 Hz, which is fine; but 16 Ohm || 1k = 15.75 Ohm gives 101 Hz, which is an audible bass rolloff with low-impedance earbuds. The fix would be more capacitance, and here the answer is genuinely no: I walked the full Kyocera AVX TPS ratings table and case B tops out at 100 uF for any rating of 6.3 V or above (only the 2.5 V and 4 V blocks offer 150/220 uF in case B, and 2.5 V is too close to the 1.25 V bias to be sound practice). Going to 220 uF means case C (6.0 x 3.2 x 2.6 mm) which does not fit the 1210 land. So: the 101 Hz corner with 16 Ohm loads is a genuine limitation of this design, and there is no same-footprint part that fixes it.
findings.risk: Switching to the 6.3 V part halves the voltage margin on a rail whose only excursion is the 2.5 V VAUD supply - still 5x the applied bias, so low risk, but there is no real reward either. Recommendation: leave CP2/CP3 exactly as they are, and record the 16 Ohm corner as a known characteristic rather than chasing it.
findings.verify_reason: The ESR analysis is right and the recommendation happens to be defensible, but the central negative claim is false. VERIFIED: CP2/CP3 = TPSB107K010R0400 (ESR 400 mOhm max @100 kHz) with 1.25 V forward bias via R19/R20 1k to AGND; TPSB107*006#0250 exists exactly as described - I found the row in the Kyocera AVX TPS ratings table: 'TPSB107*006#0250 B 100 6.3 85 4 125 6.3 10 250 0.583 0.525 0.233 1', i.e. case B, 100 uF, 6.3 V, ESR 250 mOhm, 0.583 A rms at 25 degC. Case C dims confirmed (6.00 x 3.20 x 2.60). Corner arithmetic reproduces: 32||1k = 31.0 ohm gives 51.3 Hz, 16||1k = 15.75 ohm gives 101.1 Hz. REFUTED: 'case B tops out at 100 uF for any rating of 6.3 V or above ... there is no same-footprint part that fixes it'. The first clause is true, but the conclusion does not follow, because the same table contains TPSB157*004#0250 - case B, 150 uF, 4 V, ESR 250 mOhm, 0.583 A rms - on the identical 1210 land. That single part both halves the ESR and moves the 16-ohm corner from 101 Hz to 67 Hz. The finding waved off the 2.5 V and 4 V blocks in one clause without doing the derating arithmetic. Minor: the dB sentence is garbled ('400 mOhm ... worth 0.04 dB' then 'going to 250 mOhm changes that to 0.02 dB'); 0.04 dB is the IMPROVEMENT from 400 to 250 mOhm, and the actual insertion losses are 0.11 dB and 0.07 dB. Also 220 uF case B exists only in the 2.5 V block, not in 2.5 V and 4 V as written.
findings.correction: Replace 'there is no same-footprint part that fixes it' with: TPSB157*004#0250 (Kyocera AVX TPS, case B, 150 uF, 4 V, ESR 250 mOhm max, 0.583 A rms at 25 degC) is a drop-in on the same 1210 land and moves the 16-ohm corner from 101 Hz to 67 Hz while halving ESR. It is a trade, not a free win, and the honest reason to decline it is voltage margin, not availability: the SE output swings the full VAUD rail, so the instantaneous forward voltage on CP2/CP3 can approach 2.5 V at very low frequency, which is 63% of a 4 V rating - outside the usual 50% derating rule for MnO2 tantalums, where the fitted 10 V part sits at 25%. Recommendation to leave CP2/CP3 alone therefore still stands, but on a different and more defensible basis than the one given.

findings.title: C12's DC-bias deration shortens the U17 supervisor's power-up delay by 24 % versus the value in the schematic
findings.current_part: C12 = GRM188R61E106KA73J, 10 uF 25 V X5R 0603. Net: Net-(U17-VDD), fed from SW through R58 5.1k with R63 100k to GND, supplying U17 (TPS3840DL20). This is an RC delay element, not a bypass. At the divider ratio the node sits at 0.951 x SW, so roughly 2.3 V mid-discharge, where the digitised Murata curve gives about -24 % and an effective 7.6 uF.
findings.proposal: No part change. Either annotate the schematic with the effective value, or - if the delay actually matters for the power-sequencing behaviour - re-scale R58 so the intended time constant is met with the real capacitance rather than the marked one.
findings.benefit: No power saving; this is the one place on the board where DC-bias deration changes a behaviour rather than a margin, which is exactly the class of problem the reviewer asked about. Arithmetic: tau = (R58 || R63) x C = (5.1k x 100k / 105.1k) x C = 4.852k x C. With the marked 10 uF that is 48.5 ms; with the 7.6 uF the part actually delivers at 2.3 V it is 36.9 ms - 24 % faster than anyone reading the schematic would compute. Whether 12 ms matters depends on U17's role in the VOUT5/Q5 sequencing, which is outside my domain; the point is that the schematic's number is wrong by a quarter and nothing on the drawing says so.
findings.risk: None from flagging. If the delay is re-scaled via R58, note that the deration itself moves with battery voltage (the same cap is 7.54 uF at 2.4 V and about 8.5 uF at 1.8 V), so the delay is not constant across the discharge curve either.
findings.verify_reason: The part identification and the small-signal derating are right; the headline conclusion applies the wrong capacitance to the wrong problem. VERIFIED: digikey.com/short/qd4q4f1m resolves to Murata GRM188R61E106KA73J, and the Murata datasheet page 2 gives 10 uF +/-10%, 25 Vdc, X5R, 0603, cap change rate +/-15.0%. Network confirmed from the BOM/netlist (R58 5.1k SW->U17.VDD, R63 100k U17.VDD->GND, C12 to GND, U17 CT pin unconnected - and the TPS3840 datasheet says 'For a fast reset CT pin can be left floating', so this RC really is the only timing element). Divider ratio 100/105.1 = 0.9515 and R58||R63 = 4.8525k both correct, so tau = 48.5 ms at the marked 10 uF. My own 500 dpi digitisation of the DC-bias chart gives -22.1% at 2.28 V (7.79 uF) and -24.7% at 2.4 V (7.53 uF) and -14.6% at 1.8 V (8.54 uF), so the finding's 7.54 uF and ~8.5 uF side-notes are right and its 7.6 uF main figure is very slightly pessimistic.
